prompt: You are putting an in-process LRU cache in front of a service handling many concurrent requests. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A cache-hit `get` mutates recency pointers and needs write synchronisation
options.explanation: Correct. A hit moves the node to the front, which is a write to shared pointers. Two unsynchronised `get`s can corrupt the list.

options.text: A read-write lock lets `get` calls run in parallel safely, because they only read
options.explanation: This is the trap: in LRU, `get` is not read-only. Holding only a read lock while relinking nodes is a data race.

options.text: The O(1) bounds are average-case, because they rest on hash map operations
options.explanation: Correct. With many colliding keys a hash map degrades, so the structure is O(1) on average, not in the worst case.

options.text: Swapping LRU for a heap-based LFU would keep every operation O(1)
options.explanation: A heap update costs O(log n), where n is the number of keys in the cache. O(1) LFU needs the frequency-bucket design.

options.text: `OrderedDict` and Java's `LinkedHashMap` implement the same hash-map-plus-linked-list idea
options.explanation: Correct. Both pair a hash table with a doubly linked list of entries, which is why they can do LRU in a few lines.

workedExample:
1. Look at `get`: it calls `_unlink` and `_push_front`, six pointer assignments in this implementation. So a hit is a write.
2. Hence a read-write lock gives no parallelism for hits; a mutex around this implementation is one solution; sharding and approximate eviction policies offer other designs.
3. All the O(1) claims inherit the hash map's average-case guarantee.
4. A heap keyed on count needs a possible sift when an access changes its count: O(log n), where n is the number of keys in the cache (at most 19 swaps for a million keys).
5. `OrderedDict.move_to_end` and `LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true)` are the library versions of the lesson's code.
